content: The request for peer review from the pharmaceutical industry was organized through the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association and the Developing Country Vaccine Manufacturer Network. The final recommendations, including GRADE assessments, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and other relevant components, were incorporated into the WHO Guidelines for Malaria. These were submitted for review by the Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) alongside the development of the WHO position paper published in the Weekly Epidemiologic Record. The glossary contains terms from the updated WHO malaria terminology (2021), which were reviewed and agreed upon by the Drafting Committee on Malaria Terminology, first convened in 2015. For further details on the committee, the review process, and additional notes on the glossary, please refer to the referenced document. Adherence refers to compliance with a prescribed regimen, such as chemoprophylaxis or treatment, or adherence to procedures and practices recommended by a healthcare provider. Adverse drug reaction is a harmful and unintended response to a medication occurring at doses typically used in humans. Adverse event is any undesirable medical occurrence in a person exposed to a biological or chemical product, which may not necessarily have a causal relationship with the product. Serious adverse event refers to an untoward medical occurrence in a person exposed to a biological or chemical product that results in death, requires or prolongs hospitalization, causes significant disability or incapacity, or is life-threatening, regardless of a causal relationship with the product. Aestivation is a survival process in mosquitoes, involving behavioral and physiological adaptations during periods of drought or high temperatures. Age group refers to a subgroup of a population classified by age, with the following recommended groupings: 0–11 months, 12–23 months, 2–4 years, 5–9 years, 10–14 years, 15–19 years, and ≥20 years. Physiological age in adult female mosquitoes is determined by the number of gonotrophic cycles completed, such as nulliparous, primiparous, or multiparous stages. Case, fever refers to the occurrence of fever (current or recent) in an individual. Case, imported describes a malaria case or infection acquired outside the area where it is diagnosed. Case, index is a case whose epidemiological characteristics trigger additional active case or infection detection. The term index case may also refer to the case identified as the origin of infection for one or more introduced cases. Case, indigenous refers to a case contracted locally with no evidence of importation and no direct link to transmission from an imported case. Case, induced is a case originating from blood transfusion or other parenteral inoculation of the parasite, rather than natural mosquito-borne transmission. Case, introduced describes a locally contracted case with strong epidemiological evidence linking it directly to a known imported case (first-generation local transmission). Case, locally acquired refers to a case acquired locally through mosquito-borne transmission. Case, malaria is the occurrence of malaria infection in a person confirmed by a diagnostic test to have malaria parasites in their blood. Case, presumed refers to a suspected malaria case not confirmed by a diagnostic test. Case, recrudescent is a malaria case attributed to the recurrence of asexual parasitemia after antimalarial treatment, due to incomplete clearance of the same genotype(s) that caused the original illness. This must be distinguished from reinfection and relapse (in the case of P. vivax and P. ovale). Case, relapsing is a malaria case attributed to the activation of hypnozoites of P. vivax or P. ovale acquired previously. Case, suspected malaria refers to an illness suspected by a healthcare worker to be due to malaria, typically based on the presence of fever with or without other symptoms. Case detection is a surveillance activity involving the search for malaria cases in a community. Case detection, active involves health workers detecting malaria cases at community and household levels, often in high-risk population groups. Case management encompasses the diagnosis, treatment, clinical care, counseling, and follow-up of symptomatic malaria infections. Case notification is the mandatory reporting of all malaria cases by medical units and practitioners to the health department or malaria control program, as required by national laws or regulations. Catchment area is a geographical area defined and served by a health program or institution, such as a hospital or community health center, based on population distribution, natural boundaries, and transport accessibility. Cerebral malaria is severe P. falciparum malaria characterized by impaired consciousness (Glasgow coma scale <11 or Blantyre coma scale <3) persisting for more than one hour after a seizure. Certification of malaria-free status is granted by WHO after it is proven beyond reasonable doubt that local human malaria transmission by Anopheles mosquitoes has been interrupted in an entire country for at least three consecutive years, with a national surveillance system and prevention program in place. Chemoprevention, seasonal malaria involves the intermittent administration of full treatment courses of an antimalarial medicine during the malaria season to prevent illness. The goal is to maintain therapeutic drug concentrations in the blood during periods of highest malaria risk. Chemoprophylaxis is the administration of a medicine at predefined intervals to prevent the development of an infection or its progression to manifest disease. Cluster refers to an aggregation of relatively uncommon events or diseases in space and/or time, occurring in numbers greater than expected by chance. Combination therapy is the use of two or more classes of antimalarial medicines with unrelated mechanisms of action. Coverage refers to the fraction of the population in a specific area receiving a particular intervention. Coverage, optimal is the result of a prioritization process guiding resource allocation decisions, combining impact analysis, value for money, and stakeholder engagement to outline trade-offs in intervention selection and combination. This process considers programmatic goals, context-specific factors, and equity implications. Coverage, universal health ensures that all individuals and communities receive the health services they need without financial hardship. It includes the full spectrum of essential quality health services, from promotion to prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care. Cure is the elimination of all malaria parasites causing the infection from an infected person. Cure, radical refers to the elimination of both blood-stage and latent liver infection in cases of P. vivax and P. ovale, thereby preventing relapses. Cure rate is the percentage of treated individuals whose infection is cured. Cyto-adherence is the propensity of malaria-infected erythrocytes to adhere to the endothelium of the microvasculature in the host's internal organs. Diagnosis is the process of determining the cause of an illness (e.g., a febrile episode) through clinical assessment and diagnostic testing. Diagnosis, molecular involves the use of nucleic acid amplification-based tests to detect malaria parasites. Diagnosis, parasitological refers to the detection of malaria parasites, Plasmodium-specific antigens, or genes in the blood of an infected individual. Diapause is a condition of suspended animation or temporary arrest in the development of immature and adult mosquitoes. Dosage regimen (or treatment regimen) specifies the formulation, route of administration, dose, dosing interval, and duration of treatment with a medicine. Dose is the quantity of a medicine to be taken at one time or within a given period. Dose, loading refers to one or a series of doses given at the start of therapy to rapidly achieve the target concentration. Drug efficacy is the capacity of an antimalarial medicine to achieve the therapeutic objective when administered at a recommended dose, with minimal toxicity and good tolerability. Drug resistance is the ability of a parasite strain to survive and/or multiply despite the absorption of a medicine given in doses equal to or higher than those usually recommended. Drug safety refers to the safety profile of a medicine (see Medicine safety). Drug, gametocytocidal is a drug that kills male and/or female gametocytes, preventing them from infecting a mosquito. Drug, schizontocidal is a drug that kills schizonts, either in the liver or the blood. Endemic area is an area with ongoing, measurable malaria infection incidence and mosquito-borne transmission over successive years. Endemicity, level of refers to the degree of malaria transmission in an area. Endophagy is the tendency of mosquitoes to blood-feed indoors. Endophily is the tendency of mosquitoes to rest indoors. Entomological inoculation rate (EIR) is the number of infectious bites received per person in a given unit of time in a human population. Epidemic refers to the occurrence of a number of malaria cases significantly exceeding what is expected in a given place and time. Epidemiological investigation is the study of environmental, human, and entomological factors determining the incidence or prevalence of infection or disease. Erythrocytic cycle is the portion of the malaria parasite's life cycle from merozoite invasion of red blood cells to schizont rupture. The duration is approximately 24 hours in P. knowlesi, 48 hours in P. falciparum, P. ovale, and P. vivax, and 72 hours in P. malariae. Exophagy is the tendency of mosquitoes to feed outdoors. Exophily is the tendency of mosquitoes to rest outdoors. Experimental huts are simulated houses with entry and exit traps for sampling mosquitoes entering and exiting, blood-feeding indoors (when a host is present), and surviving or dying in each sub-sample, per day or night. Fixed-dose combination is a formulation in which two antimalarial medicines are combined in the same tablet, capsule, powder, suspension, or granule. Focus, malaria is a defined, circumscribed area in a current or formerly malarious region containing the epidemiological and ecological factors necessary for malaria transmission. Gametocyte is the sexual stage of malaria parasites that can potentially infect Anopheles mosquitoes when ingested during a blood meal. Gametocyte rate is the percentage of individuals in a defined population in whom sexual forms of malaria parasites have been detected. Geographical reconnaissance involves censuses and mapping to determine the distribution of the human population and other features relevant for malaria transmission, guiding interventions. Gonotrophic cycle, mosquito refers to the period of reproductive development in the female mosquito, including host-seeking, blood-feeding, digestion of a blood meal, ovarian development, search for a breeding site, and oviposition. Gonotrophic discordance (dissociation) occurs when female mosquitoes take more than one blood meal per gonotrophic cycle. Hibernation is a process in which mosquitoes at one or several stages (eggs, larvae, pupae, adults) survive through behavioral or physiological changes during cold periods. House refers to any structure other than a tent or mobile shelter in which humans sleep. Household is the ecosystem, including people and animals occupying the same house and the accompanying vectors. House-spraying is the application of liquid insecticide formulations to specified (mostly interior) surfaces of buildings. Human landing catch is a method for collecting vectors as they land on individuals. Hyperparasitemia is a high density of parasites in the blood, increasing the risk of a patient’s condition deteriorating into severe malaria. Hypnozoite is the persistent liver stage of P. vivax and P. ovale malaria that remains dormant in host hepatocytes for variable periods, from three weeks to one year (exceptionally even longer), before activation and development into a pre-erythrocytic schizont, which then causes a blood-stage infection (relapse). Importation rate is the rate of influx of parasites via infected individuals or infected Anopheles spp. (gametocytes, sporozoites) or to the vector (mosquito). Infectivity refers to the ability of sporozoites of a specific strain of Plasmodium to be injected by Anopheles mosquitoes into susceptible humans and develop through the liver stage to infect red blood cells (“infectivity to humans”), as well as the ability of competent Anopheles mosquitoes to ingest human Plasmodium gametocytes, which undergo development until the mosquito has infectious sporozoites in its salivary glands (“infectivity to mosquitoes”). Insecticide is a chemical product (natural or synthetic) that kills insects. Ovicides kill eggs; larvicides kill larvae; pupacides kill pupae; adulticides kill adult mosquitoes. Residual insecticides remain active for an extended period. Insecticide, cross-resistance refers to resistance to one insecticide by a mechanism that also confers resistance to another insecticide, even when the insect population has not been selected by exposure to the latter. Insecticide, discriminating dose (or diagnostic dose for resistance) is the amount of an insecticide (usually expressed as the concentration per standard period of exposure) that, in a sample of mosquitoes containing resistant individuals, distinguishes between susceptible and resistant phenotypes and determines their respective proportions. Insecticide, dose is the amount of active ingredient of insecticide applied per unit area of treatment (mg/m²) for indoor residual spraying and treated mosquito nets, or per unit of space (mg/m³) for space spraying, and per unit area of application (g/ha or mg/m²) or per volume of water (mg/L) for larvicides. Insecticide, mixture is an insecticide product consisting of two or more active ingredients mixed as one formulation so that, when applied, it provides a combined effect.
